deep_why: PAGE generates increasingly severe fake anomalies by first adding noise to node features, then progressively disrupting graph connections. The core insight is that real anomalies live on a spectrum from mild to extreme, so by forcing the model to learn a ranked ordering where severe fake anomalies score higher than mild ones, it calibrates what each anomaly level actually looks like in the data. This ordering constraint ensures the model doesn't collapse all anomalies into a single decision boundary; instead, it learns to separate them by degree. Because real anomalies are rare and unlabeled, staging the fake ones from weak to strong gives the model a natural ladder to climb, teaching it to recognize subtle deviations before it sees the drastic ones. This framework lets practitioners detect the full range of graph misbehavior, not just the obvious cases.

The core insight is that user interest has two independent rhythms: a steady baseline of what someone likes over months (stable collaborative signal) and a volatile reaction to this week's trending topics and news (local context). By maintaining two separate representations—one learned from the entire historical interaction graph and another from sliding windows of recent behavior—the model captures both rhythms without one drowning out the other. The mathematical guarantee comes from keeping the signals orthogonal: the long-term branch absorbs stable patterns while the short-term branch isolates transient spikes. Because user engagement depends on both seasons and the moment, splitting the graph into global and windowed local views lets each pathway preserve its own temporal frequency. This two-track design ensures news recommendations stay fresh by riding current events while still knowing who the user fundamentally is.

When graphs lack node labels, many nodes become indistinguishable because their local structure is identical—a fundamental problem called local isomorphism. SCOUT adds synthetic features by measuring distances from each node to selected anchor points, much like using landmarks to describe location. The key is choosing the right anchors and the right number of them. SCOUT discovers this by first learning which centrality measure (degree, closeness, or betweenness) best captures importance for the specific task and graph, then using an elbow-detection trick on the ranked curve of node importance to automatically determine how many anchors are actually needed. This works because real-world networks have a heavy-tail structure where a few nodes matter enormously while most are interchangeable, so the elbow marks the point where adding more anchors yields diminishing returns. With smart anchor selection, the distance-to-anchor features become informative labels that break the symmetry and let the underlying graph model distinguish what was previously invisible.

In online advertising, the true value of a click (the money spent after clicking) arrives in fragments over days and weeks as the customer makes multiple purchases—a label that's incomplete until well after prediction must happen. The core challenge is that models trained on stale, incomplete labels will underestimate the true revenue. READER addresses this by recognizing that single-purchase clicks and multi-purchase clicks follow completely different spending patterns, so it routes incomplete labels through separate prediction branches. Each branch specializes: one learns single-purchase customers while the other handles repeat-buyers. By calibrating the incomplete label to estimate what the full final value will be, the model adjusts for the delay-induced bias. This splitting guarantee works because the two customer types have fundamentally different downstream behavior, so no single model can fairly represent both. This framework lets e-commerce platforms make smarter ad spend decisions despite the lag in seeing true customer value.

Implicit hate speech hides meaning behind layers—coded phrases, metaphors, tone—so surface-level keywords miss it. DuPL's core idea is that every hateful message contains latent semantic pieces (units of hostile meaning) that must be identified before judgment. The framework works in two phases: first, a high-recall miner aggressively extracts candidate hate components while a quick judge exits early on obvious cases, then a deliberation phase breaks down the components and reasons about each one separately before reaching a final integrated decision. This two-stage structure guarantees sound reasoning because it separates the act of finding potential meaning from the act of judging it—by forcing explicit detection and argumentation rather than end-to-end pattern matching, the model avoids the pseudo-reasoning trap where large models chase spurious cues. Because implicit hate lives in semantic depth rather than surface tokens, centering detection on explicitly mined components and structured argument transforms opaque decision-making into interpretable steps. This makes hate detection both more accurate and auditable for web moderation.

Choosing the right forecasting method for unseen time series is costly; teams typically train many models to find the best fit. AutoMTSF transforms this selection problem into a classification task: given raw data characteristics from a new series, predict which of 41 known methods will perform best. The core principle is transfer learning—a large pre-trained model encodes the new series into a comparable representation, and patterns learned from ModelPile (a massive dataset pairing time series to their best-performing methods) reveal which method class this new series belongs to. Because forecasting method performance depends predictably on data structure (trend strength, seasonality, noise level, dimensionality), these characteristics can be extracted and matched to historical evidence without expensive trial training. By building this dataset bridge and using large-model encoding plus refined temporal pattern features, the method guarantees that selection is accurate because it leans on thousands of prior observations rather than guessing blind.

Multimodal models trained on huge corpora inevitably memorize private information, but unlearning it fairly is hard because different evaluation tasks (classification, free-form generation, entity recall) require different kinds of forgetting. TAU's core insight is that trying to forget with a single objective creates trade-offs: you might suppress classification confidence but keep generating the sensitive info verbally, or you over-suppress and break unrelated knowledge. By decomposing unlearning into three task-aligned objectives that directly target the specific behaviors tested—confidence reduction for classification, refusal generation for free-form, recall suppression for cloze—each objective pulls the model in the right direction for its task. The mathematical guarantee comes from joint optimization: these objectives aren't competing when they're matched to their tasks; instead, they converge toward balanced forgetting where private info is lost across all behaviors while general knowledge survives. This alignment principle lets practitioners achieve privacy-preserving multimodal models without collateral damage.

Finding anomalies in high-dimensional streaming data at Internet scale requires both speed and robustness to imbalanced distributions (most data points are normal). ANN-TS anchors detection on the principle that anomalies are distant from normal points in high dimensions. By building a hierarchical nearest-neighbor index and scoring each point based on its neighborhood (rather than raw distance), the model gains two guarantees: the index enables fast queries without scanning all history, and neighborhood-based scoring is robust to noise and class imbalance because it compares relative distances, not absolute thresholds. The approach adapts over time through streaming updates that refresh which points count as normal, capturing concept drift as patterns evolve. Because real-world data shifts and arrives at massive scale, an approximate-nearest-neighbor foundation avoids expensive exact computation while the statistical scoring mechanism stays stable despite extreme imbalance. This makes anomaly detection both practical and reliable for production web monitoring.

Obfuscated harmful text (using leetspeak, symbol substitution, misspellings) evades detection because tokenization breaks at out-of-vocabulary characters and inference slows with auto-regressive generation. BIND solves this by working character-by-character with bidirectional context: for each position, it predicts what the true character should be based on both what came before and what comes after, then aligns these predictions. This bidirectional approach is mathematically sound because context on both sides of a corruption gives more information than one-way prediction—a character corrupted as '3' is clearer when you know the word is 'fr33nds' (context hints 'friends'). By fixing positions rather than generating sequentially, BIND avoids the compounding error problem of auto-regressive models; the fixed-position approach also handles emojis and multi-codepoint graphemes naturally. Because obfuscated text relies on maintaining visual or phonetic similarity while corrupting individual characters, bidirectional reconstruction at fixed positions precisely inverts that corruption scheme. This design makes real-time deobfuscation fast and accurate for content moderation.

Kriging infers missing sensor values by learning from nearby observed sensors, but standard methods assume a static graph structure and struggle when similarity between nodes is unclear. DKM-GA's core idea is that the graph structure itself can be learned dynamically by combining two sources of signal: predefined spatial structure (sensors are near each other) and feature similarity (observed values cluster sensibly). The diffusion framework works iteratively: each refinement step uses graph-enhanced attention to pick the most relevant neighbors based on current partial estimates, then updates the missing values using those neighbors. This creates a positive feedback loop—better value estimates reveal better neighbor relationships, which improve the next round of estimation. Because kriging's accuracy hinges on neighbor selection, learning the graph dynamically from both structure and content guarantees that relevant observations get leveraged. The iterative refinement captures the fact that inference cascades: fixing one sensor value helps constrain its neighbors, which cascades outward. This design makes spatio-temporal kriging over sparse sensor networks both accurate and adaptive to changing data quality.

Graph Transformers grow computationally expensive as graphs grow because attention considers all pairs of nodes. VecFormer solves this by replacing node-level reasoning with graph-level token reasoning: it first quantizes node features and the graph structure using learned codebooks (similar to discrete dictionary compression), converting the graph into a compact set of symbolic tokens. Attention then operates on these tokens rather than raw nodes, slashing computational complexity. The mathematical guarantee comes from quantization: a codebook compresses many nodes into a few representative codes, preserving semantic structure while discarding noise. By learning two codebooks jointly—one for features, one for structure—the method captures both what nodes are and how they relate. Out-of-distribution generalization improves because the learned codes represent core semantic types rather than specific node instances, so transfer to new graphs is natural. Working at the token level decouples the model size from input graph size, making scaling tractable while improving robustness.

Knowledge graphs used for recommendation contain noise (incorrect relationships) and task-irrelevant clutter that mislead the recommender. The framework cleans the graph by learning which edges matter for the specific recommendation task, using two complementary operations. Diffusion-based filtering denoise the graph structure—treating the graph as a noisy signal and iteratively averaging to smooth away spurious edges while preserving strong patterns. Task-specific triplet reconstruction then re-learns which relationships actually predict good recommendations by scoring edges and selectively reconstructing important ones. This two-pass approach is sound because denoising and task refinement address different problems: denoising removes corruption from any source, while reconstruction aligns what remains to the actual prediction goal. Because real-world graphs conflate multiple types of relationships (some critical, some misleading), separating cleanup from task alignment ensures both noise reduction and goal-directed pruning. With a refined graph, the recommender system sees clearer signals about which items belong together, yielding more accurate predictions.

Emotion-aware fraud detection faces a new vulnerability: adversaries manipulate emotional cues (facial expressions, voice tone, text style) across multiple channels to look legitimate while committing fraud. CEAT's core insight is that adversarial manipulation of emotions must stay consistent with semantic context—a fraudster can't simultaneously express urgency via facial micro-expressions and calm via text without the contradiction becoming obvious. By building a unified model that jointly represents emotional features and textual context, then training with context-aware perturbations that corrupt emotion signals while keeping context intact, CEAT teaches the model to notice when emotional signals drift from their context. The mathematical guarantee comes from enforcing alignment: true emotional behavior tracks with semantic meaning, so realistic perturbations must maintain this consistency. By explicitly training on context-consistent adversarial examples rather than unguided noise, the model learns to spot emotion-based lies. This framework hardens fraud detection against a new class of attacks while preserving performance on legitimate cases where emotions and context naturally align.

Real-world graphs shift when user behavior evolves or content semantics change, causing models to make overconfident predictions on out-of-distribution data. SIGHT adds interpretable uncertainty by embedding iterative, error-driven prediction—at each step, it updates graph node estimates and computes the prediction error (mismatch between expected and observed). Large mismatches reveal where the model is confused, flagging unreliable predictions. This spiking mechanism is mathematically sound because it directly observes the model's internal inconsistency: if refined estimates don't improve agreement with expectations, the model knows it lacks understanding. By running multiple refinement cycles, SIGHT exposes whether confusion is transient (resolved by more refinement) or structural (persists despite correction), distinguishing noise from genuine distribution shift. Because out-of-distribution examples violate assumptions the model learned, they generate persistent mismatch signals that standard confidence scores miss. This interpretable uncertainty mechanism lets practitioners detect when a graph recommender or classifier is seeing something it wasn't trained for, enabling safer deployment in dynamic web systems.

Continuous first-person egocentric video from smart glasses far exceeds any model's context window, making long-horizon reasoning impossible with vanilla approaches. Egocentric Co-Pilot uses Temporal Chain-of-Thought to break long questions into reasoning steps over time, then compresses context hierarchically: each time window is summarized, summaries are compressed further, building a pyramid that fits in memory. This layered abstraction works because visual reasoning about daily tasks has natural structure—moments nest into scenes (making coffee), scenes nest into activities (morning routine), activities nest into goals (get to work)—so hierarchical compression preserves decision-relevant details while discarding redundancy. By distilling continuous video into compact semantic levels, the model reasons about hours of footage within the transformer's limits. The lightweight multimodal intent layer then turns raw speech and gaze into actionable tool commands without requiring a heavy unified model for each sense. This web-native architecture (streaming via WebRTC, orchestrated by an LLM) guarantees that glasses remain always-on and responsive by offloading heavy reasoning to the cloud while keeping perception local. This design makes assistive AI practical for everyday smart-glasses use.
